Graphs are ubiquitous and are widely used to capture relationships between different entities in real-world applications. However, compared with traditional sequential data (e.g. text and audio), the unstructured property and the sparsity make processing big graphs very challenging. The course will introduce a series of data structures and algorithms for graph processing in terms of database (i.e., big data) and deep learning. Fundamental methods and the state-of-the-art research works will be integrated. The course will serve as a launching pad for those interested in graph analytics, big data processing and graph neural networks.

Data structures and algorithms are the building blocks of many complex systems and software. Certain fundamental graph algorithms such as Dijkstra's algorithm and depth-first search have been covered by many text books and compulsory courses. They may be discussed in terms of pseudocode and time complexity. This course will start from studying how to efficiently implement the fundamental algorithms in big graphs. Then, the course explores more challenging and more complex algorithms step-by-step. When dealing with big graphs, we may consider various scenarios such as external memory solutions, distributed solutions, multi-core solutions, etc.

The course also puts some attention to graph neural networks, which is a hotspot in the area of AI and deep learning. The course will not study theoretical details about machine learning and deep learning but just introduce several representative graph neural networks. The students will play with basic graph learning tasks and understand learning-based techniques for graph problems such as link prediction and node classification.

This course introduces the core concepts and technologies involved in managing Big Data. It will first introduce the characteristics of big data and big data analysis. Then, we will learn the open-source big data management framework Hadoop. We will mainly focus on Hadoop MapReduce programming. YARN, HDFS, HBase, and Hive will be briefly introduced as well. We will also learn an open-source memory-based distributed computing framework Spark. Another major focus of this course is algorithm design on large-scale data sets based on big data management frameworks, in various domains such as data stream mining, graph data processing, and finding similar items.

This course aims to introduce students to the detailed internal structure of database management systems (DBMSs) such as Oracle or SQL Server. DBMSs contain a variety of interesting data structures and algorithms that are also potentially useful outside the DBMS context; knowing about them is a useful way of extending your general programming background. While the focus is on relational DBMSs, given that they have the best-developed technological foundation, we will also consider more recent developments in the management of large data repositories.

Relational DBMSs need to deal with a variety of issues: storage structures and management, implementation of relational operations, query optimisation, transactions, concurrency, recovery, security. The course will address most of these, along with a brief look at emerging database systems trends. The level of detail on individual topics will vary; some will be covered in significant detail, others will be covered relatively briefly.

An important aspect of this course is to give you a chance to explore the internals of a real DBMS: PostgreSQL. Lectures will discuss the general principles of how DBMSs are implemented, and will also illustrate them with examples from PostgreSQL where possible. Since DBMSs are very large pieces of software, it won't be possible to explore the entire PostgreSQL system in depth.

As the amount of Web data increases, it is becoming vital to not only be able to search and retrieve this information quickly, but also to store it in a compact manner. This is especially important for mobile devices which are becoming increasingly popular. Without loss of generality, within this course, we assume Web data (excluding media content) will be in XML and its like (e.g., HTML, JSON).

If time allows, we may cover optional topics such as: streaming algorithms, text analytics, Web data optimization for mobile devices. The lecture materials will be complemented by two programming assignments and numerous tutorial-type, written exercises.

This course aims to introduce the student to core concepts and practical skills for engineering the data in Web-service-oriented data-driven applications. Specifically, the course aims to expose students to basic infrastructure for building data services on the Web, including techniques to access and ingest data in internal/external sources, develop software services to curate (e.g. extract, transform, correct, aggregate the data), develop services to apply various analytics and develop services to visualize the data to communicate effectively using data. The course uses the Python programming language as the practical basis for its modules. However, the concepts taught are universal and can be applied to any other web development language/framework.

This course will focus on the routing and switching architectures, algorithms and protocols for packet switching networks, both connectionless and connection oriented networks (such as IP and ATM networks). Advanced Internet addressing : CIDR, VPN, NAT. In depth discussion of interior and exterior routing protocols, such BGP, OSPF. IP over ATM solutions : such as LANE, Classical IP over ATM. IP switching and MPLS. Mobile IP. Internet Multicasting. Overview of emerging switching and routing technologies, such as optical routing and QoS routing. There is a substantial network programming component in the assessable material, for which C prgramming knowledge is assumed.

We live in a world that events do not happen instantly. It takes a certain amount of time to download a video from a server to your own mobile device. It takes a certain amount of time for a computer to finish the execution of an algorithm. The time to completion (or response time in performance analysis terminology) is a performance metric that computer scientists and computer engineers should be concerned about because no one wants to wait unnecessarily. If you can understand the factors that determine the response time, then you can influence those factors so that the response time becomes acceptable. This course will take a mathematical modelling and analytical approach to understand response time in computer systems and networks. The primary goal is to explore how mathematical modelling and mathematical methods can be used to model, analyse and design computer systems and networks so that they have good performance. There are three major topics that will be covered by this course:

Queuing analysis (Note: Queues are important because they give rise to waiting time.)

Discrete event simulation

Integer programming for network design

Machine learning is the algorithmic approach to learning from data. The course also covers aspects of data mining, the application of machine learning to obtain insight from data. In this course machine learning algorithms are placed in the context of their theoretical foundations in order to understand their derivation and correct application. Machine learning also is an empirical science, where performance of algorithms must be rigorously evaluated on datasets. Completion of this course will contribute to further learning in advanced topics such as deep learning, bioinformatics, computer vision, and robotics. Topics covered in the course include: linear models for regression and classification, local methods (nearest neighbour), tree learning, kernel machines, neural networks, unsupervised learning, ensemble learning, and learning theory. To expand and extend the development of theory and algorithms presented in lectures, practical examples will be given in tutorials and programming tasks during the project.

This course presents an in-depth study of statistical machine learning approaches. It aims to provide the student with a solid understanding of methods for learning and inference in structured probabilistic models, with a healthy balance of theory and practice. It will cover topics on the semantics of direct and undirected representations in probabilistic graphical models, exact and approximate inference, and learning of model parameters and structure.

In this course, we will study a class of statistical inference models known as Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs). PGMs are a great example of how Computer Science and Statistics can work together. PGMs use graph data structures to represent domains with large amounts of variables and specialised algorithms for efficient inference over these graphical models. Therefore, PGMs have pushed the limits of probability theory to the scale and rate necessary to provide automated reasoning in modern AI systems.

During this course, we will cover several graphical models, including Bayesian networks, Markov networks, Conditional Random Fields, Markov chains, Hidden Markov Models, Kalman Filters and Markov decision processes. We will have a clear understanding of how these models work as well as their main algorithms for inference and learning. We will also cover several algorithms used to learn parameters and make inferences such as Monte Carlo Markov Chains (MCMC), Gibbs Sampling, Viterbi and the Baum-Welch algorithms, among others.

Neural networks and deep learning play a critical role in pushing the boundaries of what AI can achieve, making them indispensable for various industries and applications. Their ability to learn and adapt from data has revolutionised many fields and opened up new opportunities for solving complex problems. This course provides an introduction to and deep exploration of neural networks and deep learning principles and practice.

Topics chosen from: perceptrons, feedforward neural networks, backpropagation, deep convolutional networks, image processing; geometric analysis of trained networks; recurrent networks, language processing, semantic analysis, long short term memory; deep reinforcement learning; autoencoders, generative models, adversarial training; designing successful applications of neural networks; recent developments in neural networks and deep learning.

Applied workshop in an emerging area in cyber security. The course is supervised and taught by relevant academics and/or industry experts in the field. Areas vary depending on the availability of subject domain experts from time to time. Examples of relevant areas include: Cloud Security, Cryptanalysis on commercial products, mainframe security audit and penetration testing.

This course presents some advanced topics in various aspects of artificial intelligence such as computer vision, speech and language processing, deep learning, and knowledge representation and reasoning. The course aims to integrate these various aspects of AI and present case studies where such integration of different methodologies delivers interesting applications. Project development is the major component of this course, to develop a solution to a practical or industry-based problem that requires an integration of more than one type of AI techniques ranging from symbolic AI (e.g. knowledge representation and reasoning) to deep learning, with example applications in computer vision, speech and language processing, etc. Assessment is based on group project development.

Computer vision is the interdisciplinary scientific field that develops theories and methods allowing computers to extract high-level information from digital images or videos. From an engineering perspective it seeks to automate perceptual tasks normally performed by the human visual system. Generally, vision is difficult because it is an inverse problem, where only insufficient information is available about the objects of interest in the image data. Physics-based mathematical and statistical models as well as machine-learning methods are used to assist in the task. Current real-world applications are wide-ranging, and include optical character recognition, machine inspection, retail object recognition, 3D model building, remote sensing, medical imaging, autonomous driving, motion capture, surveillance, face recognition, biometrics, and many others. This course provides an introduction to fundamental concepts and an opportunity to develop a real-world application of computer vision.

Recommender systems are information filtering and search tools for providing personalized user interaction and navigation through a complex space of products or services. The aim is to address information overload by providing users with items that better meet their needs and support their decision making. Recommender systems are important commercial tools that are widely used by e-commerce and social media companies to drive sales and user engagement. This course covers the basic types of recommender system, the main recommendation algorithms, and machine learning and natural language processing techniques used to support recommender systems.

Computing is an integral part of modern engineering. Computing is used in the design, automation, experimentation, monitoring, diagnosis, data collection, data analysis, visualisation and many other aspects of engineering. A very important skill for engineers is to be able to use computers to help them to solve problems efficiently. The aim of this course is to give an introduction to computing for engineers with an emphasis on computational problem solving. In order to realise this aim, the students will learn to use the Python programming language and some of its many packages to solve problems. Since the course is designed primarily for engineers, the computing examples are often presented together with an engineering context to help the students to appreciate the applications of computing in engineering. This course also includes a minor component in Matlab and spreadsheet.

This course is the first of the workshops series that are a key feature of the Software Engineering degree. These workshops are designed to teach students to work in teams (or groups) using agile methods and apply their theoretical knowledge to solve real-life problems. Building on foundational Software Engineering principles of first year core course COMP1531, this workshop focuses on the processes of designing and building components (APIs) of a large software application.

This workshop will offer students the opportunity to get practical experience on the activities of analysing software requirements and producing design artifacts as well as use collaborative techniques and tools to support these processes. In addition, it aims to provide students with teamwork skills and software design techniques that an engineer would use in the development process. The students will also be getting experience on different aspects of designing and developing an API microservice and a web-based application. The requirements for this course have been determined in collaboration with industry partners and will relate to developing a realistic application. The course has a number of industry sponsors that include Nine and Macquarie Bank.

This course is the last of the workshops series that are a key feature of the Software Engineering degree. These workshops are designed to teach students to work in teams using agile methods and apply their theoretical knowledge to solve real-life problems. This workshop builds on foundational Software Engineering principles of first year core course COMP1531, as well as the second-year workshop SENG2021. Students in this course are required to use modern technologies and tools that are used in industry to build robust, performant and scalable software services in the context of an enterprise DevOps environment. Alongside a development of technical maturity, students explore ideas surrounding leadership in a Software Engineering context through working in a team and individual reflection. The course has a number of industry sponsors that include Atlassian, GitHub, AWS, Optiver and New Relic.

​Evidence-based decision-making requires the ability to define problems, use data, design interventions and evaluate outcomes. This course is a fully problem-based learning experience in which you work individually and in teams as management consultants or advisors.

You will use insights from data analysis to address one of three types of problems: motivating and designing an intervention, identifying and managing risks related to interventions, or evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of interventions. The course is relevant to evidence-based decision-making in business, government and not-for-profit organisations.

As a synthesis course, it requires you to apply and integrate knowledge and skills from across your degree, complete professional reports, and communicate findings clearly.​

Economics is about shaping a better world. It examines how people, businesses, and governments make decisions with limited resources, and how those choices affect society.

In this course, you’ll learn to “think like an economist” and apply economic reasoning to real-world challenges like climate change, inequality, poverty, and access to healthcare and education. You’ll gain tools to evaluate policies, understand who benefits (and who doesn’t), and design solutions that create positive impact.

We’ll explore questions such as:

How can growth and sustainability be balanced?

What policies reduce inequality and improve welfare?

When do markets fail, and what can governments do?

By the end of the course, you’ll not only master core concepts but also know how to use them to tackle pressing issues. Whether your path is business, policy, or global development, economics offers powerful insights for building a fairer future.

Macroeconomics examines the behaviour and performance of the economy as a whole. This course explores how economists use models to understand the behaviour of key variables—output, employment, inflation, interest rates, and exchange rates—and how these models are evaluated with evidence. It also considers how governments, central banks, and international institutions in shaping outcomes through fiscal and monetary policy.

By the end of the course, students will have a clear framework for understanding how households, businesses, and governments interact, and will be able to apply macroeconomic reasoning to real issues such as recessions, growth and sustainability, building the foundation for further study in economics and related fields.

​​How can economic policy address climate and environmental pressures without ignoring other vital societal goals? This course introduces environmental economics through the lenses of markets and market failure, showing why environmental problems arise and how economists evaluate solutions. You will examine policy tools such as regulation, taxes, subsidies, and pollution permit trading, and learn methods for valuing the benefits and costs of environmental protection. The course also develops foundations in microeconomic thinking for environmental decision-making and highlights the trade-offs involved in real policy choices.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to evaluate environmental policy instruments and explain their welfare and distributional implications using economic reasoning. You will gain an appreciation for the fact that the solutions to environmental problems are rarely simple and an ability to consider other perspectives and the complexities and trade-offs inherent in environmental policy decisions.​

In today’s data-driven world, quantitative skills are essential for tackling real economic and business problems. From evaluating financial decisions to forecasting markets and assessing policy, this course is designed to give you these skills early, ensuring you can approach future studies and professional challenges with confidence.

This course will equip you with a working knowledge of the most common analytical tools and techniques in economics and business, providing the basis for further studies. Topics include the mathematics of finance, matrix algebra, probability, calculus and optimisation. Special emphasis is put on the application of concepts and techniques to typical problems in business and economics.

By the end of the course, you will know how to translate quantitative techniques into practical insights, interpret data effectively, and provide evidence-based solutions that prepare you for advanced coursework and professional applications.

In today’s data-driven world, the ability to analyse and interpret information is a core skill for economists, business leaders, and decision-makers.

This course provides the essential statistical toolkit for analysing data in economics, finance, accounting, marketing, and business. It emphasises practical application, using Excel to turn data into insights and support evidence-based decisions.

Students will learn to summarise data, understand uncertainty, and test ideas with confidence. Topics include descriptive statistics, probability distributions, parameter estimation, hypothesis testing, and regression models.

By the end of the course, students will be confident in using statistical methods to support evidence-based conclusions, a skill that is highly valued in economics, finance, accounting, marketing, and the broader field of business.

​​Understanding the big picture is the first step to making informed decisions. This course will empower students with economic principles and ideas that enable them to understand and debate how best to address pressing socioeconomic and political challenges.

You will participate in active reflection and debate about the discipline’s approaches, objectives, and limitations, about the history of economic development, and about how economics can contribute to framing and solving current challenges. Topics include economic growth and development in the long run, the relationships between political regimes and economic growth, the economics of conflict, the origin and persistence of social and economic inequalities, the exploitation of natural resources and climate change.

By the end of the course, you will be able to critically evaluate economic arguments, understand how to address real-world problems through different lenses, and apply these perspectives to contemporary policy debates and everyday decision-making.​

Decision-making by consumers, producers, and governments lies at the heart of economic analysis. It determines how scarce resources are allocated, how markets function, and how welfare is distributed across society.

The first half of this microeconomics course is devoted to the study of decision-making and the modelling of associated market behaviour. We then study how individual economic decisions interact in markets with varying degrees of competition, paying substantial attention to the comparative welfare outcomes produced by different market forms.

Additional topics include externalities, game theory and its applications, and asymmetric information. There is an emphasis on the use of analytical and mathematical models, which underpin much of current research in microeconomics.

By the end of the course, students will be able to apply core microeconomic models to analyse decision-making and market outcomes, critically evaluate efficiency and welfare implications across market structures, and use formal tools to address issues such as externalities, strategic interaction, and information asymmetries.

The macroeconomy of a country is a complex network consisting of millions of interacting agents such as consumers, firms, banks, and government institutions. This course introduces students to some of the key models economists employ to understand how these entities interact to generate economic growth, the business cycle, and inflation.

This course covers models of aggregate income determination in open economies; theories of aggregate economic behaviour with respect to consumption, investment, and financial transactions; balance of payments and exchange rate analysis; theories of inflation and unemployment; introductory dynamic analysis, and theories of growth and business cycles. The models will be applied to the data and used to analyse the observed growth patterns across the world.

By the end of the course, you will have developed the tools, skills and knowledge base necessary to operate as a practicing macroeconomist.

​​How do governments shape the business environment and influence the decisions of the businesses and individuals that interact in a market economy? This course examines the role of government intervention in the economy, including why markets left alone can fail, when intervention can be justified, and how policy choices affect societal outcomes. You ​will examine practical policy issues such as income redistribution, government-private sector interactions, and the evaluation of government programs.

​By the end of this course, you will have a firm foundation in government and policy analysis and be able to apply rigorous economic reasoning to analyse strategic interaction, policy design, and institutional choices. You will be equipped to contribute with precision and confidence to real-world policy debates.

Labour markets shape income, employment, inequality and the way people experience economic change. This course gives you theoretical and practical tools for understanding how labour markets work and how policy affects workers, firms and broader economic outcomes.

You will study labour supply and demand, wage determination, wage structures and wage differentials, labour productivity, labour mobility, discrimination, and the role of government and unions. The course also examines macro-institutional outcomes, including labour force participation and the evolution of labour markets. Drawing on international research and trends, it places particular emphasis on Australian labour market institutions, data and examples.

By the end of the course, you will be able to use microeconomic models, empirical evidence and labour market data to analyse current debates in Australia and overseas.​

​​Extreme poverty remains one of the central challenges in economic development. This course explores the causes and correlates of global poverty and investigates policies designed to improve welfare in developing countries.

The course takes a microeconomic approach, focusing on individual and household behaviour and on market failures that can lead to sub-optimal choices. You will study the measurement of poverty and inequality, the roles of health and education, credit, savings and insurance constraints, migration, environmental degradation, and child labour. You will also consider how economists assess whether development interventions are likely to improve outcomes for their target populations.

The course does not cover macroeconomic topics such as institutions, geography, growth, trade or liberalisation in depth. Students interested in those areas are encouraged to consider ECON3110 Development Economics, ECON3109 Economic Growth, Technology, and Structural Change, ECON3116 International Trade, and ECON3104 International Macroeconomics.​

Game theory is a structured way to think about strategic interactions and it is fundamental to the understanding of modern business strategy.

In this course, you will be introduced to the basic tools of Game Theory and its applications to business choices. We will cover normal form and extensive form games, games of perfect and imperfect/incomplete information, and will introduce equilibrium concepts such as Nash Equilibrium, Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium and Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium. We will also look at repeated games and the theory of reputation.

By the end of the course, you will not only be equipped with an understanding of the basic principles of strategic analysis but will also easily navigate the issues related to integrating ethical and sustainable considerations into the application of abstract theory to specific real-world business challenges.

How do you do economics experiments "right" and why is it that "the way one does an experiment is unbelievably important", as a famous behavioural economist once noted?

In this course, we will talk about the experimental method in economics—and how it differs from methods in other social sciences—and will do so by reading widely cited articles. We shall discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the experimental method relative to other empirical social science methods such as analysis of administrative data, and we will document how it can be used to explore the robustness of the "homo economicus" assumption of a rational, selfish decision-maker used in many economic models.

By the end of the course, we will find that economic theory does a good job in many applications but that there are also important behavioural deviations from the model of “homo economicus”.

What can the data tell us and how can we tell apart correlation and causality?

This course introduces the use of econometrics to explore and estimate economic relationships. Emphasis will be placed on cross-sectional data, and on understanding the conditions required for inferring causal relationships. We will tackle linear regression models, and give particular attention time series and panel data models, highlighting their relevance for economic analysis. Next, we will also consider extensions that address common data analysis complications, including heteroskedasticity, proxy variables, and other limitations. Practical computer-based exercises are integrated throughout, enabling students to gain hands-on experience with econometric software.

By the end of the course, you will have the skills to critically interpret empirical relationships and a foundation for more advanced courses in econometrics.

In an uncertain and data-rich business environment, making accurate predictions is both essential and challenging.

This course addresses how to transform data into reliable forecasts that support effective decision-making and strategic planning. It covers the practical use of econometric and statistical techniques applied in the business world. Building and evaluating forecasting models using time series data will be the focus of this course.

By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate and use reliable forecasting models based on sound economic principles.

How can we critically assess the quality and evaluate the findings of research studies in social science?

This course will provide an introduction to the most common empirical methods used in scholarship across the social sciences.

Each topic will use a research article to illustrate different empirical methods, and also the range of topics that these methods are useful for analysing. Substantive topics will include: poverty, economic growth, public health, democracy, wage determination, and education.

By the end of the course, students will be well equipped to become sophisticated consumers of empirical social science research, rather than necessarily becoming producers of that work.

​​Collusion and bargaining reveal how strategic behaviour can shape economic outcomes over time. This course provides an advanced exploration of the theoretical foundations of dynamic games and the mechanisms that drive these outcomes. Building on foundational knowledge in microeconomics and game theory, you will examine dynamic games, with a particular focus on collusion and bargaining. The course develops the analytical tools needed to understand how strategic incentives affect cooperation, negotiation and efficiency.

By the end of the course, you will have a stronger foundation for analysing dynamic strategic interaction and for evaluating the economic mechanisms that sustain cooperation and determine bargaining outcomes.

In today’s global economy, national policies and outcomes are deeply interconnected.

This course introduces the core concepts and analytical tools of open-economy macroeconomics, providing a structured framework for examining how countries interact through trade, capital flows, and policy choices. It covers exchange rate determination, balance of payments, current account imbalances, international asset markets, and the role of fiscal and monetary policy in open economies. It also considers the functioning of different exchange rate regimes, the challenges of monetary unions, and the causes and consequences of international financial crises. Emphasis is placed on applying theory to contemporary issues and policy debates, enabling students to better interpret real-world events and understand the constraints and trade-offs faced by policymakers.

By the end of the course, students will appreciate how global forces shape national economic outcomes and long-term growth prospects.

When so many economic decisions are taken by political actors, understanding the economy also means understanding the interactions between politics and economics.

This course covers theory, evidence and current issues at the intersection between economics and political science.

Topics considered include economic theories of the state, regime changes and revolutions, voting theory, interest group politics, corruption, the democratic peace, and electoral competition.

By the end of the course, you will have the skills relevant in understanding the delicate interplay between economics and politics.

​​Insurance is the oldest and most widespread form of financial risk management. Life insurers and annuity providers play a central role in modern financial markets by pooling longevity, mortality, and investment risks. The economic analysis of insurance markets draws on, and enriches, core theories of asset pricing, corporate finance, industrial organisation, and public economics.

This course uses the insurance sector—in particular life insurance and annuities—as a lens through which to understand financial economics. We begin with the institutional architecture of the insurance industry: products, balance sheets, data sources, and regulation. We then study how insurers price contracts. Next, we develop supply-and-demand models to analyse market outcomes in the variable annuity and life insurance markets and investigate how reinsurance and off-balance-sheet vehicles reshape risk. We conclude by examining insurers’ portfolio-choice decisions and their implications for asset prices and systemic risk.​

​​Why do some countries grow and prosper while others remain trapped in poverty? Poverty and underdevelopment remain central global economic challenges. This course provides an in-depth exploration of competing explanations of underdevelopment and current strategies for promoting development. You will examine the roles of institutions, institutional change, markets, and policy in shaping development outcomes, with close attention to both domestic and international contexts. A key focus is the interaction between theory and evidence, including how to assess whether specific interventions are likely to improve welfare.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse major drivers of underdevelopment, assess development policies with theory and evidence, and identify credible pathways for improving outcomes.

​​What determines who gains and who loses in global trade and how governments should respond? International trade shapes economic growth, wages, inequality, and the success or failure of businesses. This course provides a rigorous analysis of trade theory and trade policy, supported by empirical evidence. You will study comparative advantage, technology differences, factor endowments, and economies of scale, and how these forces influence trade patterns and income distribution. And you will evaluate the effects of key policy tools and develop practical problem-solving skills for trade analysis.

By the end of this course, you will be able to use trade models and empirical evidence to evaluate policy choices and their implications for key societal outcomes.​

What drives the behaviour of firms and industry dynamics in the modern economic landscape?

This course studies the behaviour of firms and industry sectors, with a focus on competition outcomes and market dynamics. Through an exploration of market structures (including perfect competition, monopoly, and oligopoly), dynamic strategic interaction, price discrimination, product differentiation, advertising, entry and predation, it connects theoretical concepts with real-world relevance.

By the end of the course, you will develop a deep understanding of the economic forces at play in real-world markets and how they come together to drive economic policy.

Organisations face recurring economic problems: how to design incentives, allocate decision rights, resolve conflict and decide what to produce internally or outsource. This course studies the internal organisation of firms and other organisations using tools from game theory, information economics and contract theory.

You will be introduced to foundational theories and then apply them to real-world managerial problems. The course examines why organisations arise in market economies, how organisational structures affect behaviour, and how economic models can help analyse incentives and conflict within organisations.

By the end of the course, you will be able to use game-theoretic models to interpret organisational problems and evaluate alternative approaches to incentives and management.

​​Standard economic theory assumes that people have correct beliefs based on correct statistical reasoning, that they are narrowly self-interested, and that they manage to maximise their utility. Decades of experimental evidence suggest a more complicated picture. People systematically misperceive probabilities, cooperate with strangers in ways that sacrifice their own material payoffs, and make choices that they themselves deem suboptimal. Explaining these empirical regularities requires new theory.

In this course, students will study the core findings of behavioural economics, learn the formal theoretical frameworks developed to explain it, and build the empirical reasoning skills needed to critically evaluate competing accounts. Topics include reference-dependent preferences and prospect theory, intertemporal choice, risk preferences, bounded rationality, social preferences, behavioural game theory, and behavioural public policy.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to formulate behavioural hypotheses precisely, evaluate them using appropriate theoretical tools, and critically assess the evidence used to support or challenge them.​

​​Health and human capital are central to individual well-being and economic growth. This course explores how natural, social, economic and political environments affect the accumulation and stock of health and human capital, and how health and human capital interact with one another.

You will examine inequalities in health and human capital across society and consider how policy may help reduce them. The course is largely empirical. It moves beyond documenting correlations, such as relationships between in-utero pollution exposure and birth weight or class size and academic achievement, to ask how researchers can identify causal relationships.

By the end of the course, you will understand key methods of causal inference in empirical research and be able to assess evidence on health, human capital and related policy questions.​

​Environmental problems are among the most important and contested policy issues. This course provides an economic perspective on those problems and on the policy tools used to address them.

You will examine why environmental problems arise, why unregulated markets may fail in environmental contexts, and how economic instruments such as regulations, taxes, subsidies and pollution permit trading schemes can respond to these failures. The course also covers methods for determining the benefits and costs of environmental preservation.

By the end of the course, you will be able to take part in environmental policy debates using economic reasoning and evidence.​

Mathematics provides the formal language of modern economics, enabling us to rigorously analyse models, clarify assumptions, and derive precise insights into how economic systems function and respond to change.

This course provides a working knowledge of basic analysis, topology, and static and dynamic optimisation techniques applied in economics. Topics include logic and set theory, topological principles in Euclidean spaces, properties of real-valued functions (continuity, concavity, quasi-concavity), differentiation in multi-dimensional Euclidean spaces, classical optimisation with and without constraints, comparative statics, and envelope theorems.

By the end of the course, you will become familiar with a wide range of mathematical techniques as illustrated within mainstream theoretical applications such as consumer theory and game theory.

​Modern econometric work increasingly draws on econometrics, data science, statistics and machine learning. This course introduces these methods through the lens of econometric theory and applications.

You will study the links between theory, computational methods and the application of models to real examples. The course develops an intermediate-level understanding of modern econometric, statistical and machine learning methods, including the theoretical justifications for their use and the practical skills needed to apply them in Python.

By the end of the course, you will be able to select and apply suitable methods to econometric modelling tasks, interpret programming output, and communicate evidence-based results for economics and business problems.​

​Financial decisions often depend on understanding how financial data behave over time. This course provides a framework for modelling financial time series data, including commodity and asset prices, interest rates and exchange rates.

You will learn the key characteristics of financial data, concepts of volatility and risk, methods for modelling time-varying volatility, approaches to risk management, and relationships among financial series. The course also develops forecasting skills for financial assets and the ability to evaluate competing forecasts.

By the end of the course, you will be able to use econometric and programming tools to model, estimate, make inferences about and forecast financial data.​

Applied econometrics provides the tools to transform raw data into meaningful economic insight. It bridges theory and evidence, allowing us to rigorously test hypotheses, identify causal relationships, and inform real-world policy and business decisions.

This course extends econometric modelling using linear regression to cover nonlinear models such as logit and probit, regression methods for forecasting, and an introduction to the treatment of endogeneity (e.g. instrumental variable estimation). Special emphasis will be placed on the process and potential pitfalls of conducting and evaluating applied econometric research.

By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the necessary knowledge to be able to conduct your own econometric research using standard real-world economic and business data.

Understanding the statistical backbone of modern econometric analysis is fundamental. It underpins how economists draw reliable conclusions from data, and critically evaluate the tools used in empirical research.

This course provides the foundations for modern econometric methods including probability theory, mathematical statistics, asymptotic theory, frequentist and Bayesian inference, underlying mathematical methods and an introduction to statistical computing. Mastering this course will give students a deeper understanding of the formal mathematical and statistical underpinnings of methods and knowledge commonly used in econometrics. Throughout the course, material will be presented in the context of simple models to concentrate on the concepts.

By the end of the course, you will have a rigorous grasp of the statistical principles that support econometric methods, providing the foundation needed for advanced data-driven economic analysis.

​​How do economists turn complex data into credible evidence for decisions? The explosion of the amount, scope and availability of data has transformed how organisations make decisions. This course examines econometric and machine learning methods suited to data-rich environments, including regression, model selection and regularisation, regression trees, cross-validation, and natural experiments. You will compare how these methods perform across description, prediction, and counterfactual analysis tasks and how the key distinction between experimental and observational data must inform your analysis. You may also be introduced to newer data types such as textual, spatial, and network data.

​By the end of this course, you will be able to apply modern empirical methods suited to a data-rich environment, critically assess identification and model choices, and communicate evidence with precision.​

​​This course will provide you with an introduction to econometrics as it is applied in macroeconomics. Emphasis is on hands-on implementation of the methods covered in the course. Topics include macroeconomic data, linear and nonlinear time series models, practical issues with likelihood-based inference for these models, forecast evaluation, structural identification and use of micro data in empirical macroeconomics.

By the end of this course, you will be able to implement core macroeconometric methods, evaluate model assumptions, and draw defensible conclusions from aggregate data in order to undertake modern macroeconomic research.​

Note: The course code for this course was previously EDST2003

This course will engage in substantive exploration of key concepts, issues, and debates in language, literacy, and numeracy education, with particular reference to the language, literacy, and numeracy demands of the school curriculum and pedagogy. It draws on current research to identify likely areas of difficulty in language, literacy, and numeracy learning and discusses effective teaching strategies for learners, including English as an additional language/dialect learners.

An introduction to the study of Educational Psychology which examines some aspects of development and of learning and instruction. Topics include: cognitive development, development of memory, the role of knowledge, problem solving and thinking, an introduction to instructional methods.

Do schools reduce or reinforce inequalities based on social, cultural, economic, and gender differences? What makes schools effective? Is education a public good or a private commodity? And what is the role of teachers, given that most research shows that schools only play a small role in explaining differences in how children do in school? By the end of this course, you should be able to discuss these four key questions. To do so, the course uses equity and social justice as key themes, and current research in educational sociology as evidence. You should complete the course with a critical understanding of how education, teachers and teaching interact with society.

As a pre-service teacher this course provides you with knowledge about language and children’s language and literacy development. It will introduce you to the socio-functional theory of language; how children learn to mean nonverbally and verbally in early childhood; and how they perceive and create meanings orally, in written language and multimodally in primary school years. You will also explore differences and diversity in language and literacy development among bilingual children and children with language development delay. This course develops your synthesis and analytical skills to gather and evaluate research information about diverse children’s language and literacy development and analyse their needs.

This course is designed to develop content knowledge that underpins the teaching of Human Society and its Environment. As a pre-service teacher you will engage with the necessary knowledge of Australian history and geography from a personal, local, national and global perspective; as well as engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander history and culture. You will develop content knowledge on the complex factors that have shaped Australia as a nation including British colonisation and Indigenous peoples, the development of democracy, and migration. You will investigate Australia’s identity through geographical concepts including place, environment, sustainability and change. You will also develop an understanding of geography as an interaction of people, places and environments across a range of scales. In this course you will develop knowledge of the skills required to acquire, process and communicate geographical information so as to better understand your role as responsibly informed global citizens. Particular emphasis will be placed on developing the skill of inquiry learning; being able to evaluate sources of data (both primary and secondary) as being reliable; identify bias and different perspectives; critically analyse findings; and draw and present conclusions using the appropriate contextual language in a range of communication forms.

As a preservice teacher, this introductory course provides you with a foundation to primary school scientific subjects and content. You will study concepts from the earth, space, biological, and physical sciences as they relate to the NSW Science K-6 Syllabus. This course also aims at developing your skills in communicating scientific findings and using technology for teaching.

As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with fundamental knowledge of The Arts in education. You will examine the basis on which learning in the visual and performing arts is grounded and the nature of students’ learning progression in the primary years of schooling. As a means for exploring and researching the disciplines of Visual Arts (including Media Arts), Music, Dance and Drama this course introduces you to a conceptual framework comprising the core and essential concepts of arts practitioner, artwork, audience and subject matter. You will learn to apply this framework in your own research of instances of arts practice and draw links to ways arts practices can be explained and interpreted. Through this research you will examine the different artforms in each discipline, how artists make artworks, how works are consumed and valued by different audiences on personal, community, symbolic and critical levels, and what artworks represent about our local, national and global societies, including Australian, Indigenous Aboriginal, Asian and international artists from historical and contemporary contexts. This course also develops your skills in critical interpretation when examining and interpreting different forms of art.

This course provides preservice teachers with fundamental knowledge about engagement with, and discussions about, mathematical concepts which have been shown to be relatively challenging for students to understand. Concepts, aligning with the NSW syllabus include: proportional reasoning that underpins understanding of fractions, decimals, percentage, scale, similarity, and probability; variation and uncertainty; and generalisation. These concepts are relevant across the number and algebra, measurement and space, and statistics and probability curriculum strands. Preservice teachers will deepen their procedural knowledge and conceptual understanding of these mathematical concepts with an emphasis on building their confidence, and appreciation of the interconnected nature of mathematical content and the role of mathematics as a critical tool to address problems of global significance as well as personal relevance.

Subject Area: Education

This course provides an opportunity for students to understand the structure and practice of education in NSW and appreciate the cognitive and societal factors that shape students' experiences and educational outcomes. Through a university-based seminar and 15 days of school-based fieldwork, the course enables students to observe and interact with a diverse range of students and professional educators and to actively reflect on the teaching and learning that is taking place in an educational institution.

Note: In order to undertake professional experience placements, you must: meet eligibility criteria; understand the policies and procedures that apply to professional experience placement; and provide satisfactory evidence of the NSW Mandatory Compliance Documentation (via InPlace).

Note: The course code for this course was previously EDST1108.

Teachers hold significant responsibilities to support, implement, respect, and learn from Indigenous perspectives in the classroom and in educational communities. In this course, you will learn how to enact this responsibility in classroom teaching, schooling, educational policy, and other professional practices. First, you will reflect on and locate yourself, your beliefs, and your perspectives as a future teacher in relation to land, language, culture, time, place, and relationships. You will then learn how this positionality impacts and informs your responsibility as a teacher, and helps you understand your students and their learning needs. Finally, you will engage with a range of Indigenous perspectives, research, theory, policy, and evidence to critically evaluate teaching resources and scenarios. This course will shape your professional practice in teaching in Australia or in other places that have their own histories of occupation, colonisation, or custodianship.

This course critically examines issues and innovations of contemporary relevance in state, national and global curricula. You will learn about the history and significance of curriculum innovations including learning progressions, general capabilities, and the integration of curriculum perspectives across disciplines and how these developments shape the role of the teacher, students, subject content and the broader purposes of schooling. Using social, philosophical and ethical frameworks you will evaluate the impact of these developments on education, discipline content, learning and teaching in the 21st century context.

Drawing on a range of contemporary motivational theories, this course considers their implications in the school context, with a focus on learning and teaching. These seminal theories serve as a foundation to an extensive empirical research base that enables students to learn about the nature of motivation in their own lives, with an emphasis on learning and educational settings. It also supports teachers to apply a range of practical strategies and techniques in their own pedagogy.

This course examines various theorizations of identity and culture, investigating how different conceptualizations of identity and culture constrain and/or enable particular educational responses to a range of sociopolitical and socioeconomic issues, at the societal, institutional, classroom and individual level.

In this course, you will improve your reading, writing and oral communication, and enhance your ability to communicate effectively with students, parents and other key stakeholders using a variety of skills and strategies. The course has a particular focus on intercultural understanding and language and literacy development for teachers new to Australian educational contexts.

As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with wide knowledge of mathematics content and mathematical applications. Special emphasis is put on your confidence, enthusiasm and finding meaning to learn, apply and teach mathematics. The course introduces you to the key mathematical concepts in the Australian curriculum, focusing on a few key understandings including reinforcing concepts considered earlier in the program (proportional reasoning, uncertainty and variation, and generalisation). You will also learn how the foundational mathematics skills can be scaffolded to move learners forward from early stages of learning towards increasingly sophisticated ideas. During the course you will become familiar with literature and learn to reflectively develop as a teaching professional.

In this course you gain new or updated skills in the specialist TESOL field. You engage with (advanced) language teaching methodology and its practical applications through a program of seminars and online interactions. Topics cover different approaches to English language learning and teaching, including effective teaching strategies and techniques for teaching reading, writing, listening and speaking, materials development, and the planning and evaluation of individual lessons and units of work. The role of ICT and the internet is addressed as an integral part of the whole course.

In this course you will be provided with knowledge and skills in the field of Creative Arts in education. Experiences in the areas of Visual Arts, Music, Dance and Drama will develop your pedagogical knowledge and understanding of the distinctive nature of each discipline. You will develop a critical appreciation of the unique contributions the arts make to society and how these contributions can be engaged with, and interpreted in, the primary school classroom. Pedagogical principles, theoretical components and practice within Music, Visual Arts, Drama and Dance are examined and applied in the design and implementation of classroom practices in school settings.

Students should have completed EDST1244 before undertaking this course.

As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with knowledge, confidence and interest to understand and use mathematical problem solving in your teaching of mathematics and to build the problem solving capacities of your students. The course introduces you to three types of mathematical problems: 1) abstract riddles that have historically entertained people and assisted the development of the thinking skills of humankind, 2) modelling problems requiring the application of mathematical theories into real life situations, and 3) interdisciplinary challenges people are facing in the future that require out of the box thinking. You will consolidate your foundational mathematics skills and become confident users of mathematical ideas. During the course you will become familiar with the intertwined development of mathematics and humankind.

In this course you will be introduced to the continuum of mathematics learning K-6, with reference to the NSW K-10 Mathematics syllabus. There will be a focus on evaluating and teaching number concepts, taking into account the range of developmental understanding and student ability prior to school entry. The emphasis will be on the pedagogical approaches and teaching strategies suitable for Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 which will develop your understanding of the three strands in the NSW Syllabus - Number & Algebra, Measurement & Geometry, and Statistics & Probability. There will also be a focus on the formative and summative assessment strategies needed to evaluate student progress in the early years.

Students should be enrolled in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program and have completed EDST2112 before undertaking this course.

In this course, you will learn how to teach children how to read. Among the range of approaches to early reading instruction, evidence best supports reading instruction that is explicit, systematic, and sequenced. Such instruction includes the components of phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, and oral language development. You will learn what these skills are, how to teach them, how to assess them, and how to respond with evidence-based interventions to develop early reading skills.

Students should have completed EDST1120 before undertaking this course. Students should not be enrolled in EDST3221 and EDST3200 before completing EDST3182.

As a pre-service teacher, this course prepares you for teaching 21st century literacy with focus on the teaching of reading and viewing of written and multimodal texts in printed and digital platforms that students from years 3-6 encounter in the English and other subject areas. For the English subject, you will be introduced to a range of children’s literary genres by Australian, Indigenous Aboriginal, Asian and international authors in conventional and contemporary media including novel, picture book, graphic novel, and film. You will also learn about key English textual concepts as well as language and multimodal resources for constructing these concepts. For other subject areas, you explore a range of factual texts and their distinctive language and visual features. Building on the subject content knowledge, you will develop your understanding of curriculum documents relating to Reading/Viewing and content pedagogical knowledge at macro (programming), meso (lesson planning) and micro (teaching delivery) levels. The course also introduces you to technological applications that can be used for teaching Reading and Viewing and pedagogies to differentiate instructions for diverse learners.

As a pre-service teacher, this course prepares you with curriculum, content and pedagogical knowledge for teaching composition of oral, written and multimodal texts in the K-6 English syllabus. You will learn about children’s writing development processes from oral language, to letter, word and text composition. You will also learn about contemporary text creating practices required in the 21st century curriculum including drafting, composing and publishing. The course also introduces you to pedagogies to assist primary school students develop their creating competence including computer assisted pedagogies. In this course, you will learn to compose model texts to be used as teaching resources, analyse and evaluate teaching resources, and develop a program for teaching and assessing writing/creating with detailed lesson plans and activities to cater for learner diversity.

This course examines the syllabus, curriculum planning, assessment strategies, classroom management and development/selection of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of human society and its environment in the primary school classroom. Students will engage in the selection/development/evaluation of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of key concepts in human society and its environment.

This course examines the syllabus, curriculum planning, assessment and classroom management strategies relevant to the teaching of science and technology in the primary school classroom. You will engage in the selection, development, and evaluation of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of science and technology in the primary (K-6) classroom. The course aims to enable you to harness children’s natural curiosities to develop interest, enthusiasm, and knowledge for science and technology.

Students should have completed EDST1200 before undertaking this course.

In this course you will build on the knowledge, skills and understanding developed in EDST3179 Mathematics 1. The focus is on Stages 2 and 3 in the NSW K-10 Mathematics syllabus. You will engage in findings from contemporary research to explore pedagogical strategies suitable for developing student understanding of numeracy; and how this understanding supports mathematical understanding across Stages 2 and 3. Formative and summative assessment strategies suitable for this age group are included, along with skills needed to identify and analyse a range of data about students’ progress. You will also consider how to support learners as they transition to Stage 4 in Mathematics.

Students should have completed EDST1311, EDST2112, and EDST3179 before undertaking this course. The course is complemented by a minimum of 5 days supervised professional experience.

As a preservice teacher, this course provides you with essential knowledge of Physical Education skill learning and primary school Health content for teaching PDHPE in the Australian classroom. Through a practical approach, the course introduces you to the 12 Fundamental Movement Skills (FMS). You will learn the theoretical underpinnings of key elements of Health and Personal Development, with a focus on sensitive topics. This course also develops your understanding of how each of the focus areas of PDHPE (Movement Skill and Physical Activity; Respectful Relationships and Safety; Identity, Health and Wellbeing; and Self-Management and Interpersonal Skills) are interrelated and how they combine to create a holistic approach to teaching PDHPE.

This course provides an overview of the field of special and inclusive education. It surveys the characteristics, training, and educational needs of students with a disability. The course emphasizes accommodating students with a disability in inclusive settings, including legal mandates and regulations; characteristics and educational needs of students with a disability; and evidence-based practices which can be used with these students in the general education classroom. By the end of the course, students will have a broad overview of the field and its key concepts, issues, and the relevant Department of Education policies. They will be conversant with the main categories of students with a disability and know some ways of accommodating for these students in the inclusive classroom.

Classroom management and student engagement is the number one concern of all new teachers. This course provides students with both the theoretical and practical applications of classroom management principles necessary for new teachers to make professional decisions with respect to classroom management concerns. The focus of this course is on creating an engaging classroom environment and on positive behaviour interventions and support, including the evidence-based practices crucial to effective classroom management.

This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the field of gifted education, delving into talent development and best practices for identifying and responding to the needs of gifted and talent students. Students will explore (a) models of giftedness, (b) domain-specific and general characteristics of gifted learners, (c) underachievement, (d) teacher responsibilities, and (e) differentiated instruction and curriculum design for all learners.

In this course you will focus on teaching the NSW PDHPE syllabus which covers physical, social, emotional, cognitive and moral development of students across K-6. You will explore key researchers and current findings in child and adolescent development, especially in relation to pedagogical issues and strategies for this age group. Integration of aspects of PDHPE in the other KLAs will be explored, along with the literacy and numeracy demands of the PDHPE syllabus.

Students should have completed EDST4002 before undertaking this course. This course is complemented by a minimum of 5 days of supervised professional experience.

This course develops pre-service teachers’ understanding of how EAL/D learners acquire and use language in primary classrooms. You will use frameworks such as the EAL/D Learning Progression and ESL Scales to analyse learner language and interpret patterns of development. The course emphasises evidence-based pedagogical decision-making, requiring you to apply research and professional knowledge to justify teaching strategies. You will design differentiated learning tasks that support language development and promote inclusive, equitable learning for diverse students.

Overall, the course prepares you as pre-service teachers to analyse learner language and design responsive teaching approaches aligned with the expectations of the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership.

This course explores differentiation in primary English to support diverse learners. As pre-service teachers, you will analyse research on literacy development and learner diversity, including EAL/D, disability, and giftedness, to inform inclusive practice. You will apply pedagogical content knowledge to design differentiated English learning sequences aligned with the curriculum, incorporating Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledges and ICT. Through case studies, you design and justify aligned teaching and assessment approaches that promote engagement and achievement. The course also examines strategies for creating inclusive learning environments and supports critical reflection on professional practice, ethical responsibilities, and evidence-based approaches to differentiation in primary English contexts.

As the world is facing a digital technology booming era, you will need to be well-prepared in terms of knowledge and skills to confidently participate in the 4.0 society. The aim of this course is to prepare you, as a pre-service teacher, for this compelling mission. You will be equipped with knowledges to integrate the learning outcomes from other curriculum areas such as Arts, Science, Technology and the Australian curriculum (v9)’s general capabilities in teaching the K-6 English curriculum. At the heart of this course is the teaching of multimodal digital literature adaptation for critical comprehension and creative composition. You will learn about key literary concepts and language and multimodal resources for realising these concepts. You will also learn to apply and critique technology assisted pedagogies for teaching critical comprehension and creative composition of literature and non-literature multimodal digital texts. The knowledge and skills gained in this course will also help you to design differentiated literacy instructions for struggling, high performing and EAL/D students by using multimodal texts for differentiated content, process and learning environment.

As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with opportunity to consider and engage with current issues in mathematics teaching. You will consider from a research perspective such things as: the evidence for and against particular pedagogical approaches to mathematics teaching that are recommended across a range of Australian educational jurisdictions; the role of technology, including AI, in teaching and learning mathematics; and the role of data, including data generated from standardised tests such as NAPLAN, school based tests, and teachers’ informal records, in informing mathematics teaching. In this course, you will gain experience in evaluating the quality of research evidence, arriving at justifiable positions on controversial issues, and articulating the research evidence for mathematics teaching practices that you intend to implement in your classroom.

This course is the first research course in the B.Ed Primary program and will provide you with an understanding of research in education. This will be achieved through exploring different research traditions, research ethics, the research process including issues of validity and reliability, a variety of both qualitative and quantitative research approaches and methodologies used in educational research, the management and analysis of data, and critical thinking and different genres of writing education research and findings. The course will prepare you for conducting your own research project including issues of identifying and formulating a research question; and selecting and applying appropriate research approaches and methods of inquiry. Successful completion of this course is one of the conditions for you to pursue your enrolment into the B.Ed Primary with embedded Honours program.

This is a hybrid course. It is available to both undergraduate and postgraduate students. The course content, delivery and assessment will be identical for both groups of students.

In this course, you will begin to learn how to teach Chinese in secondary contexts. You will use relevant syllabus documents to develop innovative and engaging lesson plans. You will learn and practise a range of effective teaching strategies designed to engage a diversity of learners in a safe and supportive classroom environment. You will learn how to use digital and other innovative resources to assess and improve learning in the discipline and to develop language, literacy and numeracy skills across the curriculum. Through self and peer evaluation you will also learn how to present yourself in a professional, supportive manner.

Professional experience is the central component of all pre-service teacher education programs. Professional Experience 2/Internship is the final capstone course in the pre-service teaching program, done concurrently with or after all other core courses. All pre=service teachers complete 8 weeks of university based classes before a 9-week (45 day) professional experience block in a NSW school. The placement begins with 3 days of structured observation followed by 22 days of closely supervised teaching, followed by 20 days of more independent teaching, taking one half of a teacher’s normal load. Professional Experience 2/Internship allows pre-service teachers to achieve the AITSL standards for a graduate teacher. It aims to develop a strong commitment, enthusiasm and respect for the teaching professions and encourages pre-service teachers to engage with the broader community.

Note: Professional Experience 2/Internship occurs at the times specified by the School of Education. In order to arrange timely professional experience placements, pre-service teachers must log in to the School of Education’s online placement system and enter requested information no later than week 2 of the term they will be completing their Professional Experience 2.
